title: Spike: Deterministic A/B assignment hash inputs (route-level experiments)
body:
Context / why this spike exists
We need a deterministic (stable) assignment function for route-level A/B testing that:
- Is stable across retries + streaming reconnects (doesn’t “flip” variants).
- Is privacy-safe (no new PII collection or logging requirements).
- Works for both Hosted + Dedicated and is feasible in the gateway + policy/routing layer.
- Is debuggable/replayable (support can reproduce “why did this request go to variant B?”).

This doc is specifically about the input(s) to the hashing/bucketing step (aka “assignment key”), and the stickiness semantics. It’s not trying to decide metric schema or experiment config modeling.

Constraints / assumptions
- Route-level experiments are configured on an API route (e.g., /v1/chat/completions) and scoped to a project/tenant.
- We already have stable identifiers available in the request context (tenant_id, project_id, api_key_id) and can optionally accept a customer-provided end-user identifier header.
- We should not depend on identifiers that are unstable (IP) or high variance (User-Agent) to avoid assignment churn.
- We do NOT want to require SDK changes for v1, but we can document an optional header that improves stickiness at the end-user level.
- We must keep exposure logs and metrics low-cardinality (hash inputs can be more granular than what we log, but we must not accidentally encourage per-user dimensions in telemetry).

Candidate hash inputs (what we considered)
1) tenant_id (aka org/workspace)
Pros:
- Always present.
- Stable and low sensitivity.
Cons:
- Too coarse: every request from the tenant will get the same assignment if tenant_id is the only key (i.e., 100% of tenant traffic becomes variant A or B depending on bucket). That defeats the purpose of traffic splitting.
Conclusion: tenant_id must be included for namespacing, but cannot be the sole key.

2) project_id
Pros:
- Always present for the API surface we care about.
- Good for namespacing; helps ensure identical user IDs across projects don’t collide.
Cons:
- Same issue as tenant_id if used alone.
Conclusion: include for namespacing but not as the only entropy source.

3) api_key_id
Pros:
- Always present (for authenticated requests).
- Stable across retries/reconnect.
- Privacy-safe from Redwood’s perspective (internal id).
- Doesn’t require customer changes.
Cons:
- Sticky at “API key” granularity, not end-user. If a customer uses one API key for all end users (common), then assignment is effectively per-tenant anyway (same churn problem).
- If a customer rotates keys, they may see assignment shift.
Conclusion: decent default fallback entropy source, but we need a better option if customers can provide an end-user identifier.

4) Customer-provided end_user_id header (proposed header: X-Redwood-End-User-Id)
Pros:
- Best approximation of “real user” stickiness.
- Solves the “single API key” problem.
- Makes experiment analysis less biased (reduces correlation between variant and cohort if routing is per-user instead of per-key).
Cons / risks:
- Privacy: even if customer-provided, this may be personal data. We must not log the raw value anywhere.
- Not guaranteed to exist. Some customers won’t have user ids (server-to-server batch workloads, agents, etc.).
- Support needs a way to reproduce assignment without seeing the raw id (see replayability section).
Conclusion: support as optional primary key, but never required. Must be processed via HMAC/hashed transform inside gateway and never emitted in telemetry.

5) Request ID (X-Request-Id) / trace id
Pros:
- High entropy; perfect splitting.
Cons:
- Not sticky across retries unless the client guarantees idempotency semantics (and even then, not universal).
- Totally breaks “same user sees same variant” expectation; might increase variance for some product experiences.
Conclusion: not suitable as the default assignment key. Might be used as a “last resort” to achieve splitting when no other entropy exists, but that changes semantics substantially (more like per-request randomization).

6) Session id / conversation id (e.g., X-Redwood-Session-Id)
Pros:
- Good for chat: keeps a conversation in one variant.
- Less privacy sensitive than user id if customer uses opaque ids.
Cons:
- Not universally available.
- Still can be PII depending on customer.
Conclusion: possible future enhancement; not required for v1. If we do it, needs clear docs and strict non-logging.

7) IP address / User-Agent
Pros:
- Available.
Cons:
- Unstable (mobile/enterprise NAT), causes “variant flapping”.
- Privacy risks; would complicate ADR-0188 stance.
Conclusion: explicitly do not use.

8) Payload-derived (prompt hash)
Pros:
- Could make experiments stable for identical inputs.
Cons:
- Very expensive; privacy nightmare; encourages logging/handling of prompt text.
Conclusion: do not use.

Recommendation: assignment key composition (v1)
We need three things in the hash input:
A) Namespacing to avoid cross-experiment interference
B) An entropy source that yields good splitting
C) A stable, replayable transform

Proposed canonical assignment input string (before HMAC):
- experiment_id
- tenant_id
- project_id
- route_id (or route template if we have it; otherwise the normalized path + method)
- subject_id (defined below)

Where subject_id selection is:
1) if request header X-Redwood-End-User-Id is present and non-empty => subject_id = "eu:" + value
2) else => subject_id = "ak:" + api_key_id
3) else (edge case; should not happen for authenticated endpoints) => subject_id = "rq:" + request_id

Important: we should not incorporate region into the assignment key for v1. Reason: it breaks stickiness when requests shift regions due to routing/failover. Instead, keep assignment independent of region, and let routing policy decide whether a variant is eligible in the region.

Why include route_id?
- Avoids surprising coupling where the same user is always in the same variant across unrelated routes. Some customers will run different experiments on different routes concurrently.
- Minimizes “spillover” effects in analysis.

Why include project_id if tenant_id is already present?
- Prevents the same end_user_id across projects from having correlated assignment.
- Future-proofs if experiments can be configured per project.

Stickiness semantics (what “stable” means)
We should be explicit about what stickiness we guarantee:
- Deterministic, not time-based: for the same (experiment_id, tenant_id, project_id, route_id, subject_id) we always return the same bucket/variant.
- No TTL-based rebucketing in v1. TTL introduces new questions (where to store state; how to handle clock skew; how to reason about “sticky for 7 days” across regions). Deterministic hashing is simpler and more debuggable.
- Variant mapping changes if and only if:
  - Experiment traffic allocation changes (e.g., 90/10 -> 50/50) OR
  - Variants are added/removed OR
  - The hashing secret/version changes OR
  - The subject_id changes (key rotation, missing end_user_id header, etc.)

If product wants “sticky for N days” later, we can do it by including an epoch component (e.g., week_number) in the hash input, but that is a product/analysis decision and should be called out as re-randomization.

Replayability / debugging goals
Support + eng need to answer:
- “Why did this request go to variant B?”
- “Is assignment working correctly for this tenant?”
- “Is the split roughly correct?”

However we cannot log raw end_user_id. Proposed approach:
- Compute assignment using HMAC-SHA256 with a server-side secret (per environment) and a versioned key id.
- The gateway/policy layer can expose a debug-only endpoint or internal tool that accepts (tenant_id, project_id, experiment_id, route_id, end_user_id OR api_key_id) and returns:
  - subject_type (end_user_id vs api_key_id)
  - hash_key_version
  - bucket (0-9999)
  - assigned variant
This tool must be access-controlled (internal only) and must not store the provided end_user_id.

Additionally, in exposure logs we can include:
- assignment_key_version (string)
- subject_type ("end_user" | "api_key")
But we should NOT include a subject hash in telemetry by default. Even a hashed user id is often treated as personal data and creates “temptation” to join across datasets. (If we ever need it for a very specific investigation, do it via targeted, time-limited debug logs behind security approval.)

Keyed hash vs plain hash
Plain SHA256(subject_id) is deterministic but makes offline enumeration attacks easier (especially if customers send emails as end_user_id, which they will despite docs). Keyed HMAC reduces this risk.
Proposal:
- assignment_key = HMAC_SHA256(secret_k, canonical_input)
- bucket = first_32_bits(assignment_key) mod 10_000 (or similar)
- key id/version is carried in config and emitted in internal logs/exposure events

Secret management
- Use existing gateway secret distribution mechanism (same class as request signing secrets). Must be consistent across regions for the same environment.
- Include key rotation plan: support two active keys (current + previous) for a period if we need non-breaking migration. Note: rotation will change assignment unless we dual-evaluate; likely acceptable only with explicit change management.

Trade-offs: per-user vs per-key stickiness
Per-user stickiness (with X-Redwood-End-User-Id) is “better” for product correctness for many apps, but it is optional. Without it, customers with a single API key effectively get per-tenant assignment, which collapses the split.
Mitigation: we can still achieve traffic splitting even without end_user_id by adding another entropy source that is stable but not per-request.
Options:
- Encourage (docs + Console warnings) adding X-Redwood-End-User-Id for user-facing apps.
- For server-to-server workloads where end_user_id isn’t meaningful, provide optional X-Redwood-Workload-Id or X-Redwood-Session-Id. (Deferred.)
- If none is present, consider using request_id as entropy. But this changes semantics to per-request randomization. I think this should be explicitly opt-in (experiment setting “assignment unit: request”) rather than silent fallback.

Concrete examples
Example A: consumer chat app
- Customer sets X-Redwood-End-User-Id: "u_83219"
- Same user sees consistent variant across retries and across devices (assuming same user id).
- Split approximates per-user split.

Example B: B2B SaaS backend job (no user id)
- Customer does not set end_user_id.
- If they use one API key for the whole tenant: assignment becomes per-tenant and split collapses.
- Solution: customer should either
  (a) use multiple API keys per “cohort” (not great), or
  (b) set an end_user_id / workload_id header derived from job id / workspace id.
We should reflect this in docs and Console warnings.

Operational concerns / edge cases
- Streaming retries / reconnect: assignment must be computed from stable fields. If clients retry with a new request_id, but same end_user_id, they still land in same variant. Good.
- Missing headers: if customer sends X-Redwood-End-User-Id sometimes but not always, they will see flipping (between end_user and api_key subject types). We should add a Console validation hint (“end-user id header not observed in last N requests”) if we can, or at minimum document in troubleshooting.
- Multi-route experiments: if experiment is truly per-route, route_id must be included; otherwise a user in variant B on one route will also be B for others, which is not always desired.
- Overlapping rollouts/canaries: not handled here, but assignment key should be purely experiment-driven; precedence decided in ADR-0187.

Suggested product/Console copy (to reduce surprises)
- During create experiment flow, show: “Assignment unit: End user (recommended) if you send X-Redwood-End-User-Id. Otherwise assignment falls back to API key.”
- Add warning when split is likely to collapse: “We have not detected end-user identifiers for this route; if you use a single API key for all traffic, the experiment may not split as expected.”

Test plan ideas (quick)
- Unit tests:
  - Same canonical_input => same bucket across process restarts.
  - Different experiment_id => different assignment.
  - Presence/absence of route_id changes assignment.
  - end_user_id vs api_key_id switches subject_type and changes bucket.
- Integration tests (gateway):
  - Retry with new request_id but same end_user_id yields same variant.
  - Streaming reconnect yields same variant.
  - Config change 90/10 -> 50/50 changes observed distribution but is deterministic per bucket.

Open questions
1) Do we want the “request_id fallback” at all, or should we fail validation when there is no end_user_id and the customer only has one api_key? (Leaning: no request_id fallback by default; keep behavior predictable.)
2) Header naming: X-Redwood-End-User-Id vs X-Redwood-User-Id. (Prefer “End-User” to clarify it’s customer’s user, not Redwood user.)
3) Should we include model/config identifiers in the hash input? (Probably no; assignment chooses a variant; variant defines model/config. Including it risks churn if variant config updates.)
4) Do we need an internal-only “assignment explain” endpoint in the assignment service, or is a local library call sufficient? (SRE/support might prefer a service for consistency.)

Next steps
- Align with ADR-0187 on final canonical input + subject_id selection.
- Align with ADR-0188 on explicit statement: we never log end_user_id; exposure events only include subject_type + key_version.
- Update assignment-core library (PR 18342) to take canonical_input fields and implement HMAC + version.
- Work with Console team on warnings/copy and a “how to enable user-level stickiness” doc snippet.
